Physical properties Crystal structure Amorphous indium oxide is insoluble in water but soluble in acids, whereas crystalline indium oxide is insoluble in both water and acids. The crystalline form exists in two phases, the cubic (bixbyite type) and rhombohedral (corundum type). Both phases have a band gap of about 3 eV. The parameters of the cubic phase are listed in the infobox. The rhombohedral phase is produced at high temperatures and pressures or when using non-equilibrium growth methods. It has a space group Rc No. 167, Pearson symbol hR30, a = 0.5487 nm, b = 0.5487 nm, c = 1.4510 nm, Z = 6 and calculated density 7.31 g/cm3. Conductivity and magnetism Thin films of chromium-doped indium oxide (In2−xCrxO3) are a magnetic semiconductor displaying high-temperature ferromagnetism, single-phase crystal structure, and semiconductor behavior with high concentration of charge carriers. It has possible applications in spintronics as a material for spin injectors. Thin polycrystalline films of indium oxide doped with Zn2+ are highly conductive (conductivity ~105 S/m) and even superconductive at liquid helium temperatures. The superconducting transition temperature Tc depends on the doping and film structure and is below 3.3 K. Synthesis Bulk samples can be prepared by heating indium(III) hydroxide or the nitrate, carbonate or sulfate. Thin films of indium oxide can be prepared by sputtering of indium targets in an argon/oxygen atmosphere. They can be used as diffusion barriers ("barrier metals") in semiconductors, e. g. to inhibit diffusion between aluminium and silicon. Monocrystalline nanowires can be synthesized from indium oxide by laser ablation, allowing precise diameter control down to 10 nm. Field effect transistors were fabricated from those. Indium oxide nanowires can serve as sensitive and specific redox protein sensors. The sol–gel method is another way to prepare nanowires. Indium oxide can serve as a semiconductor material, forming heterojunctions with p-InP, n-GaAs, n-Si, and other materials. A layer of indium oxide on a silicon substrate can be deposited from an indium trichloride solution, a method useful for manufacture of solar cells. Reactions When heated to 700 °C, indium(III) oxide forms In2O, (called indium(I) oxide or indium suboxide), at 2000 °C it decomposes. It is soluble in acids but not in alkali. With ammonia at high temperature indium nitride is formed In2O3 + 2 NH3 → 2 InN + 3 H2O With K2O and indium metal the compound K5InO4 containing tetrahedral InO45− ions was prepared. Reacting with a range of metal trioxides produces perovskites for example: In2O3 + Cr2O3 → 2InCrO3 Applications Indium oxide is used in some types of batteries, thin film infrared reflectors transparent for visible light (hot mirrors), some optical coatings, and some antistatic coatings. Both crystalline forms are wide bandgap semiconductors, possessing a direct band gap of approximately 3 eV, which is crucial for their optical and electronic applications. The rhombohedral phase, often referred to as corundum-type In₂O₃, is typically synthesized under extreme conditions of high temperature and pressure, which promotes the rearrangement of its atomic lattice into a more densely packed structure. This dense polymorph, characterized by a high density of 7.31 g/cm³, possesses precise lattice parameters and atomic arrangements distinct from its cubic counterpart, influencing its specific physical and electronic characteristics. For instance, when doped with chromium, indium(III) oxide thin films emerge as promising diluted magnetic semiconductors. These materials integrate semiconducting behavior with magnetism, making them highly attractive for emerging spintronics applications, where both charge and spin of electrons are utilized for information processing and storage. Conversely, doping with zinc yields highly conductive In₂O₃, with certain compositions even exhibiting superconductive properties at extremely low temperatures. This ability to achieve high electrical conductivity, particularly when transparent, is a cornerstone for many optoelectronic devices. text: Potamogeton friesii, known as flat-stalked pondweed, or Fries' pondweed, is an aquatic plant in the genus Potamogeton. It grows mainly in mesotrophic to eutrophic rivers, lakes, ponds and ditches, rarely in brackish water. It occurs in North America, Europe, western Asia and a few scattered locations elsewhere in Asia. Description Flat-stalked pondweed grows annually from turions and seed, producing branching plants with slender, flattened stems that are well-branched. The submerged leaves are long, rather grass-like, sessile, and translucent. The leaf tips are mucronate (i. e. with the midrib extending out of the leaf, giving a pointed appearance). Abundant turions are produced along the stem, especially in autumn as the plant disintegrates. Flat-stalked pondweed could be confused with other fine-leaved pondweeds within its range, especially Potamogeton obtusifolius but potentially also P. pusillus. The combination of open stipules, rounded tips to the leaves, dense flower spikes and a tendency to produce a mass of bushy growth at the surface all help to distinguish this plant, but use of a botanical key or flora is recommended. Potamogeton friesii is diploid, with 2n=26. Two hybrids of Potamogeton friesii have been described, with P. crispus (P. × lintonii Fryer) and P. acutifolius (P. × pseudofriesii Dandy & G. Taylor). Taxonomy Flat-stalked pondweed was first described in 1847 by the Austrian botanist Franz Josef Ruprecht. The specific name friesii commemorates the Swedish mycologist and botanist Elias Magnus Fries. It is related to other fine-leaved pondweeds such as P. obtusifolius, P. foliosus and P. pusillus. Distribution Potamogeton friesii occurs predominantly in North America (Canada, northern USA), Europe (Scandinavia, Germany, Poland, British Isles, NE and central France, Belarus, Ukraine, European Russia, Pyrenees, Carpathians), There are isolated populations in southern Europe (Corsica, N Italy, Balkans) and in Asia (N China, Russia, Japan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan). Ecology and conservation In Britain, P. friesii occurs in a range of standing water habitats including ponds, ditches, canals, sluggish rivers and shallow lakes, favouring calcareous waters. It is strictly a lowland plant and is tolerant of eutrophication, especially in rivers. Like other fine-leaved pondweeds, P. friesii probably benefits from a certain amount of disturbance to suppress competing vegetation. Flat-stalked pondweed has suffered local declines and is thought to be extinct in the Czech Republic, and is Endangered in Switzerland, and Germany. It is considered to have declined in Britain, but is still widespread, and was listed as Near Threatened in 2002. A more recent assessment for England only reassessed its status as Vulnerable, reflecting ongoing population declines. However, in the Netherlands it is considered least concern. Cultivation Flat-stalked pondweed is not presently in cultivation. Although its wide ecological tolerance suggests it may not be difficult to grow, it would probably require a deeper substrate than is usual in most ornamental ponds. It swiftly distinguished itself in the publishing landscape by presenting a curated blend of literary and genre fiction, alongside poetry, insightful essays, and captivating artwork. The magazine champions a global perspective, featuring contributions from a diverse array of authors and artists hailing from various corners of the world. History and Founding GUD Magazine emerged from the collaborative vision of its founders: Mike Coombes, Sal Coraccio, Kaolin Fire, and Sue Miller. Operating under the umbrella of GUD Publishing, Inc. , their aim was to create a platform that not only published high-quality speculative and literary work but also treated its contributors with an innovative, equitable model. From its inception, the magazine sought to bridge the often-segregated worlds of literary fiction and genre-specific narratives, fostering a space where both could thrive side-by-side. Content and Contributor Model The magazine's editorial philosophy revolves around showcasing exceptional storytelling and artistry, regardless of conventional genre boundaries. This eclectic approach is reflected in its diverse content, which ranges from hard science fiction and fantasy to introspective literary pieces and experimental verse. A hallmark of GUD Magazine's operation is its unique contributor payment structure. Authors and artists are paid semi-professional rates, a standard in genre markets, but also receive royalties, effectively making them shareholders for the issue in which their work appears. This innovative model aimed to foster a stronger sense of partnership and shared success between the magazine and its creative talent. Growth and Circulation From its earliest days, GUD Magazine experienced a remarkable surge in popularity within the literary community. Between its launch in July 2006 and January 2007, the magazine received and processed an impressive 1,871 submissions, establishing a reputation for prompt and thorough responses. This rapid growth continued, with the magazine sending out over 11,000 responses by June 2009. The peak of this activity saw a staggering 800 submissions in May 2009 alone, underscoring its significant appeal to writers worldwide. In an effort to expand its reach and experiment with accessible pricing models, GUD Magazine initiated a "pay what you want" sale in November 2009. This initiative proved highly successful, nearly doubling its circulation from 400 to 700 copies, demonstrating the community's willingness to support quality independent publishing. Availability and Editorial Structure GUD Magazine has consistently been available in multiple formats, catering to diverse reader preferences. In addition to traditional print editions, the magazine embraced digital distribution early on, offering its content in various electronic formats, including PDF, PDB, and LIT. This multi-format approach ensured wide accessibility for a global readership. The magazine's editorial oversight has been managed by a rotating team of editors, with different individuals overseeing specific issues, contributing to a dynamic and varied editorial voice over the years. Recognition and Awards Throughout its publication history, GUD Magazine has garnered significant critical acclaim and industry recognition. It has been a recipient of, or received nominations for, several prestigious awards in the speculative fiction and literary fields, including the Sidewise Award for Alternate History, Australia's Aurealis Award, and the Ditmar Award. In 2008, its commitment to supporting writers was acknowledged by Writer's Digest, which listed GUD as one of the "Top 100 Markets for Magazine Writers and Book Writers, " further cementing its standing as a respected and sought-after venue for literary and genre talent.

text: Snow Hill Tunnel is a railway tunnel underneath Birmingham city-centre. It runs for 635 yards (580 metres), linking Birmingham Moor Street station at its southern end, with Birmingham Snow Hill station at its northern end. It is a vital link in the cross-city Snow Hill Lines. History The tunnel was opened in 1852 by the Great Western Railway as part of its London Paddington to main line. It was built using the cut and cover method as far as Temple Row, and then a deep cutting to Snow Hill. In 1872 the cutting from Temple Row to Snow Hill was roofed over and the Great Western Arcade built on top. Bank of England siding At the Snow Hill end of the tunnel, a short siding existed within the tunnel, alongside which was an underground entrance to the Birmingham branch of the Bank of England. The siding was used to transport cash and bullion by train to and from the bank, a facility which was last used in the mid-1960s. The bank entrance is now sealed up. Bottleneck As traffic into Snow Hill station grew, the twin tracked tunnel became a capacity bottleneck. This proved to be a problem when Snow Hill station was rebuilt and expanded in the 1900s. It was not economically feasible to widen the tunnel, as this would have required demolition of prime city-centre buildings whose foundations impeded construction. The capacity problem was therefore solved by building Moor Street station as a terminus at the southern end of the tunnel, in order to allow local trains from the south to terminate there instead of Snow Hill. Closure and reopening Snow Hill station was run down and closed under the Beeching axe in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Services south from Snow Hill were ended in 1968, and the tunnel was closed to all traffic. The last train passed through on 2 March 1968. Trains from the north continued into Snow Hill until the station was closed in 1972. Having been derelict for over 19 years, the tunnel was reopened in 1987, when a new station at Snow Hill was built. Also, Moor Street station at the southern end of the tunnel was re-sited, with two new through platforms built adjacent to the tunnel mouth. These replaced the previous terminus platforms which were then closed once the tunnel was reopened. Shortly before it opened to traffic, a charity walk through the tunnel took place, where members of the public were allowed to walk through the tunnel, from Moor Street to Snow Hill, in return for a donation to charity. The tunnel was officially reopened on 5 October 1987, along with the new Snow Hill and Moor Street stations. The growth in traffic into Snow Hill meant that the old capacity bottleneck problem resurfaced. This led to the reopening of two of the terminus platforms at Moor Street in 2010, allowing some Chiltern Railways expresses to terminate there instead of Snow Hill. text: The Clear Script (, ; , , , (), or just todo) is an alphabet created in 1648 by the Oirat Buddhist monk Zaya Pandita for the Oirat language. It was developed on the basis of the Mongolian script with the goal of distinguishing all sounds in the spoken language, and to make it easier to transcribe Sanskrit and the Tibetic languages. History The Clear Script is a Mongolian script, whose obvious closest forebear is vertical Mongolian. This Mongolian script was derived from the Uyghur alphabet. The Clear Script was developed as a better way to write Mongolian, specifically of the Western Mongolian groups of the Oirats and Kalmyks. text: {{Short description|Empirical equation used to calculate the maximum allowable vapor velocity in vapor-liquid separation vessels. }} {{About|the equation}} The Souders–Brown equation is an empirical correlation fundamental to chemical engineering, primarily utilized for determining the maximum superficial vapor velocity permissible in vapor-liquid separation equipment. Named after its originators, Mott Souders and George Granger Brown, this equation plays a critical role in the design and optimization of various process units, including flash drums, knockout drums, compressor suction drums, and the critical sizing of trayed fractionating and absorption columns. Principle and Application At its core, the Souders–Brown equation addresses the challenge of efficient phase separation. In a typical vertical vapor-liquid separator drum, a mixed-phase stream of liquid and vapor enters the vessel. Gravity dictates the separation: the denser liquid phase falls to the bottom of the drum, forming a liquid pool, while the less dense vapor phase rises and exits from the top. The efficiency of this separation hinges on the vapor velocity; if the vapor travels too rapidly, it will entrain liquid droplets, leading to carryover and potential operational issues downstream, such as equipment damage or product impurity. Conversely, a velocity that is too low would necessitate an unnecessarily large and costly vessel. The equation provides a means to calculate the maximum velocity at which vapor can travel upwards without significant liquid droplet entrainment. This calculated velocity, in turn, directly influences the required cross-sectional area and thus the diameter of the separation vessel. For instance, a common design for these separators is a vertical pressure vessel, often exhibiting a length-to-diameter ratio of approximately 3 to 4. Such designs typically aim to provide sufficient residence time for the liquid, often around 5 minutes of liquid inventory between the normal operating level and the bottom of the drum. Standard inlets include a feed nozzle, usually positioned around the half-full level, a vapor outlet at the top, and a liquid outlet at the bottom. To further minimize liquid carryover, many designs incorporate a de-entraining mesh pad or vane pack near the vapor outlet. The Equation The Souders–Brown equation is expressed as: ${\displaystyle v = k {\sqrt {\frac {\rho {L} - \rho {V}}{\rho {V}}}}}$ Where: ${\displaystyle v}$ = maximum allowable superficial vapor velocity (e. g. , in m/s or ft/s) ${\displaystyle k}$ = Souders–Brown empirical constant, often referred to as the "k-factor" (e. g. , in m/s or ft/s) ${\displaystyle \rho {L}}$ = density of the liquid phase (e. g. , in kg/m³ or lb/ft³) ${\displaystyle \rho _{V}}$ = density of the vapor phase (e. g. , in kg/m³ or lb/ft³) The k-Factor The k-factor is an empirical constant that accounts for various design and operational parameters, including the type of internals (e. g. , mesh pad, vane pack, or none), fluid properties, and operating pressure. Its value is critical for accurate vessel sizing. Recommended values of the k-factor vary significantly with operating pressure and specific application: For typical applications with a mesh pad, the k-factor generally ranges from approximately 0.107 m/s (0.35 ft/s) at near-atmospheric pressure (0 bar gauge) down to 0.065 m/s (0.21 ft/s) at higher pressures (e. g. , 105 bar gauge). This decrease at higher pressures accounts for the increased density and potential for entrainment of liquid droplets. Adjustments are necessary for specific fluid systems; for instance, applications involving foaming liquids like glycol or amine solutions often require a significantly reduced k-factor to mitigate foaming and ensure effective separation. * Separators designed without a de-entraining mesh pad will necessitate a much lower k-factor (e. g. , 0.03 m/s to 0.06 m/s) to compensate for the absence of this mechanical separation aid, thus requiring a larger vessel diameter to achieve the same separation efficiency. The mechanical design of the vessel itself, including considerations for pressure, temperature, and materials of construction, follows standard pressure vessel design codes and practices, complementing the hydraulic sizing determined by the Souders–Brown equation.

text: Temple Anshe Hesed is a Reform synagogue located at 5401 Old Zuck Road in Erie, Pennsylvania. The congregation is affiliated with the Union for Reform Judaism. History Anshe Hesed, once spelled as Anschai Chesed, "was incorporated on 23 May 1862 and organized as a classical Reform congregation on October 24, 1875, making it one of the oldest Reform communities in Pennsylvania. " The synagogue's name literally means "people of benevolence" (or kindness) in Hebrew. In his history of the region, Samuel Bates reports that eight to ten members of this congregation began meeting in 1858. Members first met in an upstairs room at the corner of Fifth Street and French Street (the Lyons property) and subsequently met in temporary facilities on French Street, Holland Street, State Street; and then at another location on French Street. Built in 1882, the congregation's first synagogue was "a brick structure trimmed in stone and an ornament to the city". The land was purchased and the synagogue was built for a total cost of $13,000. It was located on the north side of West Eighth Street, between Myrtle Street and Sassafras Street. At the time Samuel Bates published his history, the membership of Anshe Hesed was 35. The Tenth Street location was dedicated on 27 June 1930. The Temple moved to its current location at 5401 Old Zuck Road in 2018. Rabbis and prominent members of the congregation Fourteen rabbis have served Anshe Hesed. Rabbi Weil served the congregation for about a year. Rabbi M. Wertzel, also known as M Wurzel, then served the congregation twice for a total of approximately fourteen years. He was followed by Rabbis Fuld, Dr. Flengel, Levi, and Stemple. Rabbi Max C. Currick served the longest at 47 years (1901 to 1948). The most recent to serve have been Rabbis Randall M. Falk, Leonard Zion, Bernard Perlmuter, Lewis Littman, Bradley N. Bleefeld, Samuel Weinstein, Michael L. Feshbach, John L. Bush, and, from 2015 to 2018, Emily Ilana Losben-Ostrov. Emily Ilana Losben-Ostrov was Anshe Hesed's first female rabbi and the first female rabbi in the Erie area. The current rabbi is Robert Morais. Mr. B. Baker was the first president of the congregation. As one of the congregation's oldest members, Mr. Baker laid the cornerstone of the first synagogue in 1882. Cemetery Erie's earliest Jewish cemetery, which is now called the Anshe Hesed Cemetery, was founded in 1846. It is located a block west of Erie Cemetery on West 26th Street between Cherry Street and Poplar Street. text: Distocyclus conirostris is a species of glass knifefishes found in the deep waters () of the Amazon basin, lower portions of the Potaro River and in major parts of the Rio Orinoco. They are typically relegated to flood basins, flooded forests and main river channels. They have often been found gathering in small groups around vegetation, indicating a social nature. The fish has semi-translucent, glass-like pectoral and anal fins. The main body is a ground-like color with a lighter head. The largest currently recorded specimen is 34.5 cm (9.65 inches). Ecology Distocyclus conirostris has a tapering, conical snout with the top and bottom jaws being equal in length. The mouth is located terminally. The eyes are located on either side of a bilaterally compressed, elongated body and are covered by a nictitating membrane. The snout contains a uniquely small nasal capsule for the family Sternopygidae. The mouth of Distocyclus conirostris contains a single row of teeth located on the anterior area of the dentary bone, a trait also unique to this species in comparison to the other members of the Sternopygidae. The fish is covered in cycloid scales and typically has 4 to 5 gills with 4 to 11 small gill rakers. The body lacks any dark bands running laterally down the body, something present in Japigny kirschbaum, another species of the Sternopygidae. The fish also typically has 13–14 precaudal vertebrae, differing significantly from the 20–26 precaudal vertebrae present in the Sternopygus genus. Distocyclus goajira, a potential sister fish of Distocyclus conirostris, is currently a subject of debate in regards to its phylogenetic position and relationship within either the Distocyclus genus or the Sternopygidae family. Behavior Distocyclus conirostris are social fishes who communicate through the use of chirps and modulation of said chirps. These chirps are created by the fish's electric organ, which releases chirps of varying frequencies dependent on social context. It is currently unknown whether or not jamming avoidance response is utilized when encountering other weakly electric knifefish in order to decrease interference between their electrolocation accuracy and their electrocommunication usage. It is unknown whether these chirps are sexually dimorphic or whether they vary individually. Reproduction There is little information on specific reproduction of Distocyclus conirostris currently and it is unknown if their use of chirping for communicative purposes is uniquely modulated during spawning season or to reproductive means. Conservation Distocyclus conirostris is considered to be of Least Concern by an IUCN 3.1 assessment conducted in 2009. text: An accessory pathway is an additional electrical connection between two parts of the heart. These pathways can lead to abnormal heart rhythms or arrhythmias associated with symptoms of palpitations. Some pathways may activate a region of ventricular muscle earlier than would normally occur, referred to as pre-excitation, and this may be seen on an electrocardiogram. The combination of an accessory pathway that causes pre-excitation with arrhythmias is known as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Accessory pathways are often diagnosed using an electrocardiogram, but characterisation and location of the pathway may require an electrophysiological study. Accessory pathways may not require any treatment, but those causing symptoms may be treated with medication including calcium channel antagonists, beta blockers or flecainide. Alternatively, the electrical conduction through an accessory pathways can be abolished using catheter ablation, potentially offering a permanent cure. Mahaim pathways The most common sites for accessory pathways are connections between muscle tissue in the atria and the ventricles (atrio-ventricular pathways), bypassing the atrioventricular node. Rarer sites include connections between atrial muscle and the conducting tissue within the ventricles (atrio-fascicular pathways), between the atrioventricular node and the muscle tissue of the ventricle (nodo-ventricular pathways), and between the conducting tissue of the ventricle and the ventricular muscle (fasciculo-ventricular pathways). These rarer accessory pathways are sometimes collectively referred to as Mahaim pathways or Mahaim fibres. Mahaim pathways are typically seen on the right side of the heart, with their ventricular connection lying within or close to the right bundle branch. The fibres often conduct slowly and in one direction only - from the atria to the ventricles (antegrade conduction); not from the ventricles to the atria (retrograde conduction). Unlike most atrio-ventricular accessory pathways which conduct electrical impulses at a relatively fixed speed, conduction through a Mahaim pathway varies according to how rapidly it is stimulated. More frequent stimulation leads to slower conduction, known as decremental conduction. If conduction to the ventricles occurs solely through the pathway (maximal pre-excitation), as occurs during arrhythmias like antidromic atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia, the ECG appearance is of QRS complexes with a left bundle branch block morphology which can be mistaken for ventricular tachycardia. However, due to their slow decremental conduction, during sinus rhythm the 12-lead ECG will often show little pre-excitation. References Cardiac arrhythmia Heart

text: Accessory Pathway An accessory pathway constitutes an anomalous electrical connection within the heart that bypasses its normal, intricate conduction system, thereby creating a potential substrate for various cardiac arrhythmias. text: In trade finance, forfaiting is a service providing medium-term financial support for export/import of capital goods. The third party providing the support is termed the forfaiter. The forfaiter provides medium-term finance to, and will commonly also take on certain risks from, the importer; and takes on all risk from the exporter, in return for a margin. Payment may be by negotiable instrument, enabling the forfaiter to lay off some risks. Like factoring, forfaiting involves sale of financial assets from the seller's receivables. Key differences are that forfait supports the buyer (importer) as well as the seller (exporter), and is available only for export/import transactions and in relation to capital goods. The word forfaiting is derived from the French word forfait, meaning to relinquish the right (in this case, the exporter's right to receive payment from the customer — the importer). Characteristics The characteristics of a forfaiting transaction are: Credit is extended to the importer for a period of between 180 days and seven years. The minimum bill size is normally $250,000, although $500,000 is preferred. The payment is normally receivable in any major convertible currency. A letter of credit or a guarantee is made by a bank, usually in the importer's country. The contract can be for either goods or services. At its simplest, the receivables should be evidenced by a promissory note, a bill of exchange, a deferred-payment letter of credit, or a letter of forfaiting. Pricing Three elements relate to the pricing of a forfaiting transaction: Discount rate, the interest element, usually quoted as a margin over LIBOR. Days of grace, added to the actual number of days until maturity for the purpose of covering the number of days normally experienced in the transfer of payment, applicable to the country of risk. Commitment fee, applied from the date the forfaiter is committed to undertake the financing, until the date of discounting. The benefits to the exporter from forfaiting include eliminating political, transfer, and commercial risks and improving cash flows. The benefit to the forfaiter is the extra margin on the loan to the exporter. text: Forfaiting Forfaiting is a specialized form of trade finance that facilitates the export and import of capital goods and services by providing medium-term financing and assuming the associated financial risks. Distinct from traditional lending, forfaiting involves the outright purchase of future payment obligations from an exporter, typically without recourse. This mechanism essentially transforms a deferred payment sale into a cash transaction for the exporter, significantly mitigating various risks inherent in international trade. Mechanism and Scope At its core, a forfaiter – often a bank or a specialized financial institution – provides financing to the importer by discounting promissory notes, bills of exchange, or other debt instruments issued by the importer and guaranteed by their bank. The forfaiter then assumes all the commercial, political, and transfer risks associated with the transaction, effectively taking on both the importer's payment risk and the exporter's non-payment risk. In return for this service, the forfaiter charges a margin, typically incorporated into a discount rate applied to the value of the receivables. A key characteristic is the use of negotiable instruments, which allows the forfaiter to further mitigate risk by potentially reselling these obligations in a secondary market. Unlike factoring, which often deals with short-term, recurring receivables and typically covers only commercial risks, forfaiting is specifically tailored for larger, medium-term transactions, particularly those involving capital goods like machinery, industrial plants, or infrastructure projects. It benefits both the buyer (importer) by providing extended credit terms and the seller (exporter) by offering immediate liquidity and risk offloading. Key Characteristics and Terms Forfaiting transactions are characterized by several defining features: Credit Period: Typically ranges from 180 days to up to seven years, reflecting the long-term nature of capital goods investments. Minimum Value: Transactions usually involve a significant sum, with a minimum bill size often around US$250,000, and preferably above US$500,000, to make the process economically viable for the forfaiter. Currency: Payments are generally made in major convertible currencies (e. g. , USD, EUR, JPY, GBP) to minimize currency exchange risks. Security: The transaction is almost always secured by a robust instrument, such as an irrevocable letter of credit or a bank guarantee issued by a reputable bank in the importer's country. Pricing for a forfaiting deal is determined by a combination of factors: a discount rate (reflecting interest rates, country risk, and credit risk), a small number of "days of grace" (to account for potential payment delays), and sometimes a commitment fee charged from the time the forfaiter commits to the deal until the drawdown. Benefits and Industry Development For exporters, the primary benefits of forfaiting include the elimination of credit risk, country risk, interest rate risk, and foreign exchange risk. It also improves cash flow, simplifies balance sheets by removing contingent liabilities, and allows exporters to offer competitive credit terms without tying up their own capital. For forfaiters, the incentive lies in earning attractive margins for assuming these specialized risks. The global forfaiting market is supported by dedicated industry associations. VEFI (Vereinigung für Forfaitierung – Association for Forfaiting), founded in 1978, stands as one of the oldest such organizations. The International Trade & Forfaiting Association (ITFA), established in 1999, plays a crucial role in developing business relationships, promoting best practices, and advocating for the industry's interests worldwide. These organizations underscore the vital role forfaiting plays in facilitating global trade and investment, particularly in sectors requiring substantial, long-term financing solutions.

text: Legionella longbeachae is one species of the family Legionellaceae. It was first isolated from a patient in Long Beach, California. It is found predominantly in potting soil and compost. In humans, the infection is sometimes called Pontiac fever. Human infection from L. longbeachae is particularly common in Australia, but cases have been documented in other countries including the United States, Japan, Greece and the UK. The infection can be very serious, often leading to hospitalisation and sometimes death. Like other Legionella species, person-to-person transmission has not been documented, but unlike other species, the primary transmission mode has not been proven, but likely is inhalation or aspiration of dust from contaminated compost or soil that contains the organism causing legionellosis. Modes of transmission include poor hand-washing practices after gardening, long-term smoking, and being near dripping, hanging flower pots. Awareness of a possible health risk with potting mix protected against illness. Inhalation and ingestion are possible modes of transmission. Exposure to aerosolized organisms and poor gardening hygiene may be important predisposing factors to L. longbeachae infection. Compost and potting mix warning labels Compost must be handled with care, damped down with water to reduce dust before handling, and use of a face mask covering the nose and mouth to reduce the risk of inhaling the dust is needed, especially for those at high risk from infection. Studies advocate the introduction of an industry standard that ensures the use of face masks when handling potting mix and attaching masks and warning labels to potting mix bags sold to the public. Compost packaging in Australia has an L. longbeachae warning label. The New South Wales state government recommends that people reduce exposure to potting mix dust by following the manufacturers' warning present on potting mix labels, including: Wetting down the potting mix to reduce the dust Wearing gloves and a P2 mask when using potting mix Washing hands after handling potting mix or soil, and before eating, drinking or smoking Symptoms Early symptoms include fever, chills, headache, shortness of breath, sometimes dry cough, and muscle aches and pain. Most people who breathe in the bacteria do not become ill. The risk of disease is increased with increased age and smoking, and in people with weakened immune systems. text: Legionella longbeachae Legionella longbeachae is a Gram-negative bacterium belonging to the genus Legionella, widely recognized as an opportunistic human pathogen. First identified in Long Beach, California, this species distinguishes itself from the more commonly known Legionella pneumophila by its prevalent environmental reservoir and specific epidemiological patterns. Discovery and Habitat Legionella longbeachae was originally isolated in the early 1980s. Unlike L. pneumophila, which often thrives in engineered water systems like cooling towers and hot tubs, L. longbeachae is predominantly found in natural and horticultural environments. Its primary ecological niche is commonly identified as potting soil, compost, and other decaying organic matter. This widespread presence in gardening materials contributes significantly to its unique transmission pathways. Clinical Manifestations Infection with Legionella longbeachae can lead to a serious respiratory illness known as Pontiac fever, a non-pneumonic form of legionellosis. This acute, self-limiting influenza-like syndrome is characterized by a rapid onset of symptoms, typically including fever, chills, headache, shortness of breath, and debilitating muscle aches (myalgia). While generally less severe than Legionnaires' disease (a form of pneumonia caused by some Legionella species), Pontiac fever can still be highly incapacitating. Epidemiological data indicates a notable prevalence of L. longbeachae infections, particularly in Australia, though cases have been reported in various countries globally, underscoring its international public health relevance. Transmission and Risk Factors The primary mode of transmission for Legionella longbeachae is through the inhalation or aspiration of contaminated dust particles aerosolized from potting soil or compost. When dry, these materials can release microscopic particles containing the bacteria, which are then readily breathed into the respiratory tract. Several factors increase an individual's susceptibility to infection: Poor Hand Hygiene: Inadequate hand-washing after gardening or handling contaminated soil can facilitate direct transfer to mucous membranes. Smoking: Smokers are at a significantly higher risk due to compromised respiratory defenses. Immunosuppression: Individuals with weakened immune systems, whether due to medical conditions, medication, or advanced age, are more vulnerable to developing symptomatic illness. Exposure to Aerosols: Any activity that generates dust from contaminated soil, such as mixing dry potting mix, poses an elevated risk. While exposure to L. longbeachae is relatively common, most individuals do not develop illness. However, the elderly, smokers, and those with underlying health conditions or compromised immunity face a substantially increased risk of severe outcomes. Prevention Given its environmental ubiquity, preventing L. longbeachae infection largely revolves around minimizing exposure to contaminated aerosols during gardening activities. Recommended preventative measures include: Dampening Potting Mix: Always moisten dry potting mix before use to suppress dust generation. Personal Protective Equipment: Wear protective gloves to prevent skin contact and a P2 (or N95 equivalent) particulate respirator mask to filter airborne dust. Hand Hygiene: Thoroughly wash hands with soap and water immediately after handling potting soil, compost, or garden materials. In Australia, public health authorities have implemented measures such as mandatory warning labels on compost and potting mix packaging, alerting consumers to the potential risks and advising on safe handling practices to mitigate the spread of this important pathogen.

text: The Ohio and Mississippi Railway (earlier the Ohio and Mississippi Rail Road), abbreviated O&M, was a railroad operating between Cincinnati, Ohio, and East St. Louis, Illinois, from 1857 to 1893. The railroad started in 1854 and paralleled the Cincinnati and Whitewater Canal. Its East St. Louis terminal near the Mississippi River was completed in 1857. The dorsal surface is a bright red, orange-red or brownish-red in colour, with three longitudinal white lines and up to fifty white transverse rings, while the underside is paler. The dorsal white line runs from the white snout region while the two lateral white lines start at the first transverse ring. There is no ventral white line as is the case in the otherwise similar Tubulanus superbus. The first transverse rings are far apart from each other while the remaining rings are closer together and approximately equidistant. It often secretes a silken mucous tube to which sand grains and other particles stick. Distribution and habitat The range includes the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, the North Sea and the Mediterranean Sea as well as both Atlantic and Pacific coasts of North America. Early years Pierre-Louis Tribert was born in Paris on 23 June 1819, son of Pierre Tribert, deputy for Deux-Sèvres. His mother was Catherine Lecointe-Puyraveau, the daughter of Michel Mathieu Lecointe-Puyraveau, a member of the National Convention representing Deux-Sèvres who had voted for the death of Louis XVI of France. He was a brilliant student at the Bourbon College, and then spent some time at the University of Berlin. He traveled in Europe, Egypt and North America. A landowner at Saint-Denis (Deux-Sèvres), he built a public school at his own expense. Politician Tribert stood for election to the legislature on 1 June 1863 as an independent for the second riding of Deux-Sèvres, coming second with 7,382 votes against 10,772 for the official candidate M. Lasnonier, who was elected. In the elections of 24 May 1869 he stood again, and again was defeated by M. Lasnonier. When the Franco-Prussian war began, on 15 August 1870 he enlisted at the age of 52 in the 95th infantry regiment. He fought at Chevilly and at l'Hay, and was taken prisoner at Ville-Evrard on 21 December 1870. He was interned at Neisse in Silesia. In his absence, he was elected to the National Assembly on 8 February 1871. Tribert sat in the center left, participated in several commissions. He fought a duel in 1873 with a Bonapartist journalist about and article on Lecointe-Puyraveau, his maternal grandfather. On 13 December 1875 the National Assembly elected him senator for life. Although he did not belong to any political group, Tribert often voted with the Republican left. He was against the abolition of judicial tenure, against the expulsion of the princes, in favor of the Lisbonne law restricting the freedom of the press, and in favor of the high court action against General Boulanger. Pierre-Louis Tribert died in his property of Puyraveau in Saint-Denis, in Deux-Sèvres, on 15 June 1899 at the age of seventy nine. On 24 March 1908 Louise Tribert, 30-year-old daughter of Senator Tribert, married the journalist and traveler Félix Dubois. They were to have five children. text: The Union des Femmes du Niger (UFN) was a women's organisation in Niger, which was active from 1959 to 1974 and was affiliated to the Nigerien Progressive Party. It advocated, with limited success, for increases in women's rights. History The Union des Femmes du Niger (UFN) was established in 1959 and its patron was Aïssa Diori, the wife of the, at that time, future President Hamani Diori. It was preceded by the Association des Femmes, which had been established in 1956 as an alliance of women from Niamey. However many felt that organisation was too elite and the UFN was intended to be more inclusive. It was an affiliation of the Nigerien Progressive Party. By 1962 the president of the UFN was the teacher Fatou Djibo; both vice-presidents were also teachers. Another prominent member was the entrepreneur Jeannette Schmidt Degener. Niger has a long tradition of women's networks, and the UFN expanded the kind of work undertaken to include political demands. The overarching goal of the organization was equality between women and men. The UFN promoted the education of women, the improvement of sanitary facilities and the creation of women-specific jobs. It was also one of the financial supporters of the Nigerien National Museum. The UFN was unsuccessful in its demands for legislative reforms on marriage law and the bride price. As part of their lobbying, the UFN also called for the Diori government to reform divorce law, "reducing men's ability to unilaterally divorce their wives" and create fairer circumstances for child custody. UFN members also tried to get on the list of candidates for the parliamentary elections of 1970, in fact not a single woman was represented on it. The UFN called on the government to create jobs for women, including calls for a female police force. The Union des Femmes du Niger ended with the military coup of 15 April 1974, in which all existing political structures were dissolved. Under the rule of the Supreme Military Council, a successor organisation was founded in 1975 - the Association des Femmes du Niger. text: Syllabic Octal and Split Octal Syllabic octal and split octal are historical numerical notations that emerged during early computing to represent binary data in a more human-readable format, predating the widespread adoption of hexadecimal. While both leverage the octal (base-8) system, they addressed different data lengths and contexts distinctly. Syllabic Octal Syllabic octal was a specialized notation primarily employed by English Electric with their KDF9 mainframe computer in the mid-1960s. Designed to represent 8-bit values, it used three octal digits. The first octal digit encoded the two most significant bits (limiting it to values 0-3). The subsequent two digits represented the remaining six bits, behaving as a standard two-digit octal number. For instance, the 8-bit value 10110010 (decimal 178) would be 262 in syllabic octal: 10 (binary 2) formed the first digit, and 110010 (binary 50, or octal 62) formed the subsequent two. Colloquially known as "silly octal" or "slob-octal, " its unique grouping, distinct from a pure 3-bit per digit octal interpretation of an 8-bit byte, contributed to its nickname. Split Octal Split octal served a different purpose: representing 16-bit memory addresses, particularly where memory was addressed in 8-bit segments or "pages. " It was prominently used by Heathkit (e. g. , PAM8, HDOS for the H8 computer in the late 1970s) and Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC). This notation divided a 16-bit address into two distinct 8-bit octal numbers, typically separated by punctuation like a dot (. ), slash (/), or hyphen (-). For example, the 16-bit address 1001001011010100 (binary) might be expressed as 222.650 in split octal (where 10010010 is octal 222 and 11010100 is octal 650). This segmented format offered a perceived advantage in representing memory blocks, distinct from a single, contiguous octal or hexadecimal value. The utility of both notations waned with the evolution of computer architectures and the increasing dominance of hexadecimal (base-16) as the preferred shorthand for binary data, particularly with the advent of processors like the Z80. Hexadecimal's direct correspondence to 4-bit nibbles made it efficient for byte-addressable systems, as two hex digits perfectly represent an 8-bit byte, a common data unit. text: The Liberal and Democratic Union (LDU) was a South Australian political party formed by early liberals, as opposed to the conservatives. It was formed in 1906 when liberal party structures were becoming more solid. Later in 1910 after the election, the parties merged and formed the Liberal Union with Peake as leader. text: Oliguria Oliguria, also known as hypouresis, is a medical condition characterized by an abnormally low production of urine. This diminished urinary output serves as a critical indicator of various underlying physiological disturbances, ranging from mild dehydration to severe organ dysfunction. While the precise quantitative definition can vary slightly, oliguria is generally identified when urine volume falls below 400–500 milliliters per 24 hours in adults, or less than 0.5 mL/kg/h. A more severe manifestation, anuria, signifies a virtual absence of urine production, typically defined as less than 80–100 mL per 24 hours. Etiology and Classification The causes of oliguria are broadly categorized into three principal types based on the location of the contributing factor: Prerenal Oliguria: This is the most common form, resulting from insufficient blood flow (hypoperfusion) to the kidneys, without direct damage to the renal tissue itself. Conditions like dehydration, hypovolemic shock (due to significant fluid loss), heart failure, or severe burns can reduce the volume of blood reaching the kidneys, thereby decreasing filtrate formation. Renal Oliguria: Arising from direct damage or disease within the kidneys, this type often points to acute kidney injury (AKI) or chronic kidney disease. Causes include acute tubular necrosis (ATN), glomerulonephritis, or nephrotoxic drug exposure. The kidney's ability to filter waste and produce urine is directly impaired. Postrenal Oliguria: This occurs when there is an obstruction to the outflow of urine from the kidneys, anywhere from the renal pelvis to the urethra. Common culprits include kidney stones, blood clots, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) in men, or external compression of the ureters by tumors. Clinical Significance Oliguria is not a disease in itself but rather a crucial sign necessitating prompt medical evaluation. It frequently signals acute kidney injury or serves as an early warning of circulatory collapse. Urinary tract infections (UTIs), especially severe ones, can also contribute to reduced output. In postoperative patients, decreased urine production is common due to fluid shifts, hormonal responses (like increased ADH secretion), and anesthetic effects, though persistent oliguria requires careful monitoring for kidney complications. In infants, the definition of oliguria is typically set at less than 1 mL/kg/h. However, it is important to note that isolated oliguria in infants is less frequently attributed solely to kidney failure and often reflects hydration status or other systemic issues. Early diagnosis and identification of the underlying cause are paramount for effective management and prevention of more severe kidney damage or systemic compromise.

It is a -story wood-frame structure, with a side-gable roof, central chimney, and clapboarded exterior. Windows are 9-over-6 sash, with simple framing. An ell extends to the east side of the building. On the interior, the right side parlor has exposed unchamfered beams, while the left parlor has a Second Period fireplace mantel. text: Tamil Nadu Lok Adalat: A Beacon of Alternative Dispute Resolution The Tamil Nadu Lok Adalat, also known as the Tamil Nadu State Legal Services Authority, is a pioneering statutory and autonomous institution designed to provide an alternative mechanism for dispute resolution. Operating under the framework of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, it is a cornerstone in India’s quest to fulfill its constitutional promise of "ACCESS TO JUSTICE FOR ALL. " With its emphasis on amicable settlements and a people-centric approach to justice, the Tamil Nadu Lok Adalat has become a vital tool in streamlining the judicial process, ensuring justice is not only delivered but also accessible, affordable, and expeditious. --- Historical Foundation and Legal Framework The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, enacted by the Government of India, laid the foundation for Lok Adalats as an alternative form of dispute resolution. These platforms were conceptualized to address the limitations of conventional court systems, such as prolonged pendency of cases, high legal fees, and procedural complexities. The Tamil Nadu Lok Adalat follows this mandate, offering a pro-people adjudication process where disputes are resolved with minimal formality and without the necessity of stringent adherence to procedural laws or evidentiary requirements. The Tamil Nadu Lok Adalat embodies the Gandhian philosophy of reconciliation and dialogue. By promoting settlements that are voluntary and mutually agreeable, it bridges the gap between adversarial litigation and community-driven conflict resolution. Emphasis is firmly placed on conciliation rather than confrontation, which is both time-saving and cost-effective for disputing parties, particularly those hailing from rural and marginalized backgrounds. --- Structure and Jurisdiction The Tamil Nadu Lok Adalat operates at multiple levels to ensure wide-reaching access to justice. Its structure is tiered into State Lok Adalats, High Court Lok Adalats, District Lok Adalats, and Taluk Lok Adalats, catering to cases of varying legal significance and geographical spread. Each Lok Adalat has jurisdiction to hear and settle disputes ranging from pending litigation cases to pre-litigation disputes. It has the mandate to preside over both civil cases and compoundable criminal cases, including but not limited to: - Matrimonial disputes (such as divorce and maintenance). - Land partition suits. - Cases involving damages or compensation claims. - Disputes arising from public utility services like electricity, water, sanitation, and transport. - Labour disputes and motor vehicle accident claims. To bring a case before the Lok Adalat, one fundamental criterion must be satisfied: mutual consent of the disputing parties. If no settlement is achieved, the case may be referred to a Permanent Lok Adalat, which has exclusive jurisdiction over disputes pertaining to public utility services, even in the absence of mutual agreement between parties. --- Simplified Processes and Binding Outcomes The Tamil Nadu Lok Adalat is unique in its departure from conventional trial procedures. Designed to foster efficiency and accessibility, these adalats dispense with rigid adherence to procedural laws such as the Civil Procedure Code (CPC) or the Indian Evidence Act. Instead, they rely on the principles of natural justice, ensuring disputes are resolved fairly while adhering to the law's spirit, if not its letter. Decisions taken by the Lok Adalat carry the legal sanctity of a civil court decree. These verdicts are final, binding, and not subject to appeal under the regular judicial system. However, parties dissatisfied with the resolution retain the right to initiate fresh litigation in a formal court. This dual benefit of finality and flexibility has contributed to the growing trust and credibility associated with the Lok Adalat in Tamil Nadu. --- Major Milestones and Case Studies Over the years, the Tamil Nadu Lok Adalat has gained substantial recognition for its commitment to expeditious justice delivery. It has successfully resolved thousands of cases, alleviating the burden on conventional courts while fostering peace and harmony among disputants. These cases ranged from property-related matters to motor accident claims, settling disputes that otherwise might have lingered in the court system for years. This event showcased the Lok Adalat's proficiency in addressing diverse and complex issues within a fraction of the time taken by traditional courts. Success in Rural Tamil Nadu In the district of Villupuram, another notable Lok Adalat session facilitated the amicable settlement of 1,310 cases, achieving a combined settlement amount of Rs 13.57 crore. This instance not only demonstrates the financial impact of Lok Adalats but also underscores their ability to penetrate rural areas, where legal literacy and access to formal courts often remain limited. text: Karabakh Movement The Karabakh movement, also known as the Artsakh movement, was a pivotal national campaign that emerged in the late 1980s and early 1990s, fundamentally reshaping the political landscape of the South Caucasus. Rooted in the aspirations of the Armenian people, this mass movement sought the unification of the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast (NKAO)—a predominantly Armenian-populated region located within Soviet Azerbaijan—with Soviet Armenia. Although initially framed as a constitutional and cultural initiative within the Soviet Union, the movement ultimately became intertwined with the broader push for Armenian independence, culminating in significant geopolitical changes and the outbreak of the First Nagorno-Karabakh War. Historical Background Nagorno-Karabakh had long been a contested territory with deep historical and cultural significance for Armenians. Despite its majority Armenian population, the region was placed under the jurisdiction of Soviet Azerbaijan in the early 1920s as a result of Soviet territorial policies. Over the decades, simmering tensions surfaced periodically, fueled by grievances over economic neglect, cultural suppression, and perceived discrimination against the Armenian population in the NKAO. By the late 1980s, the winds of Glasnost and Perestroika, ushered in by Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, presented new opportunities for political expression. It was within this evolving atmosphere of reform that the Karabakh movement emerged, initially championed as a peaceful and lawful effort to realign the borders of the Soviet republics in favor of Armenian self-determination. The Rise of the Movement The Karabakh movement formally began on February 13, 1988, when Armenians in the NKAO capital of Stepanakert held the first demonstrations demanding the unification of Nagorno-Karabakh with Armenia. These protests struck a deep chord with Armenians both in the region and across Soviet Armenia, quickly evolving into a coordinated, grassroots-inspired national movement. Just days later, on February 20, 1988, the NKAO’s Supreme Soviet Council officially requested that the oblast be transferred from Azerbaijan to Armenia—a bold move that galvanized public rallies and further electrified public opinion. In parallel, growing ethnic animosities led to violence. On February 22–23, clashes broke out between Armenians and Azerbaijanis near the town of Askeran, marking the first episodes of unrest. These confrontations were soon followed by the Sumgait pogrom (February 27–29), in which Armenian residents of the Azerbaijani town of Sumgait were brutally attacked in a wave of ethnic violence. The pogrom left many dead and thousands displaced, forcing a mass exodus of Armenians from Azerbaijan and further intensifying hostilities. Key Events and Transformation of the Movement By the spring of 1988, the movement had gained momentum far beyond Nagorno-Karabakh itself. On March 22, over 100,000 demonstrators gathered in Yerevan—the largest protest in Armenian history at the time—to demand unification. However, just a day later, the Soviet leadership in Moscow rejected the demand, insisting that territorial changes were inadmissible under Soviet law. Despite this setback, the movement persisted, gaining symbolic victories, such as the raising of the Armenian tricolor in Yerevan on May 28, 1988, for the first time in nearly seven decades. By June 15, 1988, the Supreme Council of Soviet Armenia overwhelmingly voted in favor of unifying with the NKAO. This decision marked a watershed moment, as it represented the Armenian leadership’s formal endorsement of the movement. However, tensions escalated further, and the following months saw escalating political pressures, massive demonstrations, and retaliatory acts of repression by authorities. On December 10, 1988, key members of the Karabakh Committee, a group of intellectuals and activists who had been leading the movement, were arrested and exiled to Moscow. Their imprisonment sparked outrage and only deepened public resolve, as demonstrated by the massive November 7, 1988 rallies in Yerevan. The movement also had its share of tragedies, as Armenian communities in Azerbaijan faced increasing violence. In January 1990, the pogrom of Armenians in Baku, the Azerbaijani capital, resulted in hundreds of deaths and forced the remaining Armenian population to flee, fueling the broader diaspora and solidifying the view among Armenians that coexistence under Azerbaijani governance was untenable. The Path to Independence The dynamics of the Karabakh movement shifted as the Soviet Union began to unravel. In Armenia, the movement’s political leadership coalesced into the Pan-Armenian National Movement (HHSh), which won the 1990 parliamentary elections and pressed for sovereignty. On August 23, 1990, the Supreme Council of Soviet Armenia declared the republic's intention to become independent, marking a decisive break with Moscow. Meanwhile, in Nagorno-Karabakh, the push for self-determination culminated in the region’s unilateral declaration of independence on September 2, 1991, as the Nagorno-Karabakh Republic (Artsakh). This declaration, although politically symbolic, was not recognized internationally and set the stage for open military conflict. Legacy and Consequences The Karabakh movement, with its roots in a peaceful call for unification, ultimately escalated into full-scale war. The First Nagorno-Karabakh War, lasting from 1991 to 1994, left thousands dead and displaced hundreds of thousands on both sides. The conflict remains unresolved to this day, with periodic clashes continuing to erupt. Despite its tragic outcomes, the Karabakh movement became a defining moment in Armenia’s modern history, sparking a new era of national identity and independence. It also epitomized the challenges of self-determination within a fractured multinational system like the Soviet Union, casting a long shadow on regional stability. Today, the movement is remembered as both an assertion of collective resilience and a harbinger of enduring conflict in the Caucasus.

text: Anti-Jewish boycotts are organized boycotts directed against Jewish people to exclude them economical, political or cultural life. Antisemitic boycotts are often regarded as a manifestation of popular antisemitism. 19th and early 20th century boycotts In Hungary, agitation for boycotts began in 1875 with an antisemitic speech from Győző Istóczy in the Hungarian House of Representatives. From the 1880s there were calls in some of the Catholic press for Jews to be boycotted. The government passed laws limiting Jewish economic activity from 1938 onwards. In Russia, after a series of anti-Jewish pogroms in the Russian Empire following the assassination of Tsar Alexander II, towards that end in 1880 they were forbidden from purchasing land or taking mortgages (see the May Laws). Quotas limited Jewish access to educational institutions and from 1892 they were banned from participation in local elections and could constitute no more than 10% of company shareholders. In 19th century Austria, Karl Lueger, an antisemitic mayor of Vienna who inspired Hitler, campaigned for a boycott of Jewish businesses as a last resort for his party. Jews were only allowed to live in Vienna from 1840. An organization called the Antisemitenbund campaigned against Jewish civil rights since 1919. Austrian campaigns tended to heighten around Christmas and became effective from 1932. In Ireland, Father John Creagh in Limerick campaigned against the town's small Jewish community in 1904, leading to a boycott of Jewish businesses and the departure of the Jewish population from the town. In Ukraine, there was a boycott of Jews in Galicia, alleging Jewish support for Poland, while Poles in Galicia boycotted Jews for supporting Ukraine. In 1921, the German student union, the Deutschen Hochschulring, barred Jews from membership. Since the bar was racial, it included Jews who had converted to Christianity. The bar was challenged by the government leading to a referendum in which 76% of students voted for the exclusion. In Quebec, French-Canadian nationalists organized boycotts of Jews in the thirties. Fascist boycotts The Nazi boycott of Jewish businesses in Germany took place on 1 April 1933 as a response to the Jewish boycott of German goods which had started soon after Adolf Hitler was sworn in as Chancellor on 30 January 1933. It was the first of many measures against the Jews of Germany, which ultimately culminated in the "Final Solution". It was a state-managed campaign of ever-increasing harassment, arrests, systematic pillaging, forced transfer of ownership to Nazi party activists (managed by the Chamber of Commerce), and ultimately murder of owners defined as "Jews". In Berlin alone, there were 50,000 Jewish owned businesses. By 1945 they all had Aryan owners. In Poland, the Endeks (founded by Roman Dmowski) organized boycotts of Jewish businesses across Poland. Polish universities placed growing limits on the number of Jews allowed to attend, (see numerus clausus) and increasingly forced them to sit separately from non-Jewish students, a practice known as "Ghetto benches" which became law in 1937. In 1936 Prime Minister Felicjan Sławoj Składkowski called for "economic struggle" and "economic boycott of the Jews became formal government policy from June 4, 1936". Kosher slaughter was banned in Poland in 1936, in Germany in 1930 following the similar legislation enacted in many other European countries. In the US, Nazi supporters, such as Father Charles Coughlin (an Irish immigrant), agitated for a boycott of Jewish businesses. Coughlin's radio show attracted tens of millions of listeners and his supporters organized "Buy Christian" campaigns and attacked Jews. Ivy League Universities restricted the numbers of Jews allowed admission. Anti-Zionist boycotts In Palestine, the Arab leadership organized boycotts of Jewish businesses from 1929 onwards, with violence often directed at Arabs who did business with Jews. A series of riots in Egypt described by one British Embassy official as "clearly anti-Jewish" occurred in 1945, starting on the date of the Balfour Declaration. In the following weeks, the Egyptian press attacked Egyptian Jews as capitalists, white-slave traders, and other slurs while calling for a boycott of Jewish goods. Later in 1945, the Arab League began a boycott of Jewish businesses in British Mandatory Palestine. In the 2000s, the BDS movement, which advocates for a total boycott of Israeli products, is regarded by some Jewish civil rights organizations (such as the Anti-Defamation League and the Simon Wiesenthal Center), as well as pro-Israel organizations and scholars as driven by antisemitism. text: Anti-Jewish Boycotts: A Historical Overview Anti-Jewish boycotts have long served as an instrument of exclusion, often intertwined with societal antisemitism, aimed at marginalizing Jewish communities across various economic, political, and cultural spheres. These organized efforts gained traction in the 19th century and proliferated globally during the early 20th century, fostering systemic discrimination and exacerbating hostilities against Jewish populations. From grassroots movements propelled by local leaders to state-sponsored campaigns under fascist regimes, the history of anti-Jewish boycotts underscores the persistent challenges faced by Jewish communities throughout modern history. Early Roots and European Incidents Hungary The seeds of organized anti-Jewish boycotts took root in Hungary in 1875, following Győző Istóczy's incendiary antisemitic speech in parliament. Istóczy's rhetoric ignited widespread agitation, particularly within the Catholic press, where calls for economic exclusion of Jews found an eager audience. This sentiment only deepened in the 1930s as the Hungarian government adopted restrictive antisemitic laws starting in 1938. These measures, which profoundly limited Jewish participation in economic and cultural life, were part of a broader trend of exclusionary policies modeled after other European nations. Russia In Imperial Russia, anti-Jewish policies gained momentum following the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in 1881, an event that triggered significant political and social upheaval. The response from the Russian authorities was severe and discriminatory, culminating in the enactment of the May Laws. These decrees imposed harsh restrictions on Jewish life, including prohibitions on landownership, quotas on education, and bans on holding local government positions or owning companies. These policies, combined with periodic pogroms, forced many Jews into poverty and spurred mass emigration to escape the hostile environment. Austria Vienna, the once-vibrant multicultural capital of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, became a focal point for anti-Jewish boycotts under the leadership of Mayor Karl Lueger in the late 19th century. Lueger's populist platform made antisemitism a cornerstone of his political rhetoric, and his campaigns explicitly encouraged boycotts of Jewish businesses. The Antisemitenbund, a group devoted to opposing Jewish civil rights, intensified these efforts, particularly during the Christmas season when calls to avoid Jewish-owned stores gained traction among the populace. Ireland In 1904, Ireland witnessed its own episode of anti-Jewish exclusion. Father John Creagh, a Catholic priest in Limerick, delivered a sermon condemning the local Jewish population, accusing them of exploiting the Christian community. His inflammatory words instigated a boycott of Jewish-owned businesses, leading to widespread intimidation and economic hardship. The sustained harassment forced most of Limerick’s small Jewish community to flee, leaving a dark chapter in Irish history. Ukraine and Poland Tensions between Poles and Ukrainians in the early 20th century also spilled over into anti-Jewish boycotts. In Ukraine, both groups targeted Jews as perceived intermediaries or economic rivals, organizing boycotts that exacerbated Jewish marginalization. Poland, meanwhile, saw the rise of the Endeks (National Democrats), a nationalist party that led anti-Jewish boycotts and propagated exclusionary policies. Universities introduced "ghetto benches" to segregate Jewish students, while enrollment quotas severely limited their access to higher education. Germany The Nazi regime in Germany escalated anti-Jewish boycotts to an unprecedented level. Beginning with a nationwide boycott of Jewish businesses in 1933, the campaign quickly evolved into systematic persecution under the umbrella of state policy. Jewish-owned businesses were forcibly "Aryanized, " with ownership transferred to non-Jews, and public sentiment was manipulated to ostracize Jews from all facets of society. This economic warfare set the stage for the eventual horrors of the Holocaust, as exclusion gave way to violence and mass murder. United States Anti-Jewish sentiments and boycotts were not confined to Europe. In the United States during the 1930s, Nazi sympathizers like Father Charles Coughlin promoted propaganda encouraging Americans to boycott Jewish businesses. Simultaneously, many Ivy League universities implemented restrictive quotas on Jewish students, significantly limiting their pursuit of academic and professional opportunities. Fascist and Anti-Zionist Movements Palestine and the Arab World The struggle over land and identity in British Mandatory Palestine fueled boycotts against Jewish businesses as early as 1929. Palestinian Arab leaders organized campaigns to economically isolate Jewish communities, sometimes resorting to violence against fellow Arabs who maintained business ties with Jews. In 1945, Egypt experienced riots targeting Jewish communities, as nationalist fervor intertwined with anti-Zionist sentiments. That same year, the Arab League formalized a boycott against Jewish businesses, laying the groundwork for decades of economic isolation that would stretch into the modern era. The BDS Movement In the early 21st century, the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement emerged as a global activist campaign advocating for a boycott of Israeli products, institutions, and companies. While the movement attributes its actions to opposition to Israeli policies, critics have raised concerns that its rhetoric and actions mirror historic patterns of antisemitism. Observers argue that the campaign contributes to a broader climate of hostility toward Jewish communities worldwide. Legacy and Reflection The history of anti-Jewish boycotts reveals a persistent thread of exclusionary practices woven into the fabric of global history. While often cloaked in the rhetoric of nationalism, economic self-interest, or political ideology, these boycotts functioned as mechanisms to dehumanize and marginalize Jewish individuals and communities. Their enduring legacy serves as a somber reminder of the need for vigilance against prejudice and the commitment to fostering inclusive societies.

text: In linguistics, a conservative form, variety, or feature of a language is one that has changed relatively little across the language's history, or which is relatively resistant to change. It is the opposite of innovative, innovating, or advanced forms, varieties, or features, which have undergone relatively larger or more recent changes. Furthermore, an archaic form is not only chronologically old (and often conservative) but also rarely used anymore in the modern language, and an obsolete form has fallen out of use altogether. A conservative linguistic form, such as a word or sound feature, is one that remains closer to an older form from which it evolved, relative to cognate forms from the same source. For example, the Spanish word caro /'karo/ and the French word cher /ʃɛʀ/ are both adjectives meaning dear or beloved that evolved from the Latin word cārum /'ka: rum/. The Spanish word, which is more similar to the common ancestor, is more conservative than its French cognate. A language or language variety is said to be conservative if it has fewer new developments or changes than related varieties do. For example, Icelandic is, in some aspects, more similar to Old Norse than other languages that evolved from Old Norse, including Danish, Norwegian, or Swedish, while Sardinian (especially the Nuorese dialects) is regarded by many linguists to be the most conservative Romance language. Recent studies regarding the stability of modern Icelandic appear to confirm its status as "stable". Therefore, Icelandic and Sardinian are considered relatively conservative languages. Likewise, some dialects of a language may be more conservative than others. Standard varieties, for example, tend to be more conservative than nonstandard varieties, since education and codification in writing tend to retard change. Writing is generally said to be more conservative than speech since written forms generally change more slowly than spoken language does. That helps explain inconsistencies in writing systems such as that of English; since the spoken language has changed relatively more than has the written language, the match between spelling and pronunciation is inconsistent. A language may be conservative in one respect while simultaneously innovative in another. Bulgarian and Macedonian, closely related Slavic languages, are innovative in the grammar of their nouns, having dropped nearly all vestiges of the complex Slavic case system; at the same time, they are highly conservative in their verbal system, which has been greatly simplified in most other Slavic languages. English, which is one of the more innovative Germanic languages in most respects (vocabulary, inflection, vowel phonology, syntax), is nevertheless conservative in its consonant phonology, retaining sounds such as (most notably) and (th), which remain only in the Germanic languages of English, Icelandic and Scots, with also remaining in the endangered Elfdalian language. In the 6th century AD, Classical Arabic was a conservative Semitic language compared with Classical Syriac, which was spoken at the same time; Classical Arabic strongly resembles reconstructed Proto-Semitic, and Syriac has changed much more. Compared to closely related modern Northeastern Neo-Aramaic, which is not necessarily directly descended from it, Classical Syriac is still a highly archaic language form. Georgian has changed remarkably little since the Old Georgian period (the 4th/5th century AD). A roughly analogous concept in biology is living fossil.
